newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: NZ dollar rally seen as unsustainable - analysts.
newsitem.headline: NZ dollar rally seen as unsustainable - analysts.

text.p: New Zealand's high flying kiwi dollar pushed to its highest in more than eight years on Tuesday but some analysts said it may be poised for a dive.

It touched 71.46 U.S. cents in early trade and hit 68.08 on a trade-weighted basis, measured against a basket of currencies -- its highest levels since mid-1988. The kiwi was floated in 1985 and reached a post-float high of 72.75 cents in June 1988.

Market analysts said there is really only one thing fuelling the kiwi -- high real interest rates. A tidal wave of New Zealand dollar euro and samurai issues has seen an inflow of over NZ$6 billion swamp New Zealand this year.
However, analysts say that exporters can't cope with the 43 percent rise of the kiwi since January 1993 and some companies may soon be facing layoffs.

"I personally don't think it is sustainable for any country to manage such a rapid appreciation in its currency that we have seen in New Zealand, post-election," said Westpac Bank's Head of Financial Markets, Chris Rand.
"I don't think any country can manage it, particularly one whose exports are just under 70 percent primary produce."
One of the ironies of the kiwi's rise is that it has soared in the wake of an inconclusive general election 10 days ago. Negotiations are expected to take weeks, possibly months.
Even when a government is formed, markets expect looser fiscal policy and a widening of the central Reserve Bank's 0-2 percent inflation target.
That is likely to coincide with an easing in monetary policy, possibly when the Reserve Bank issues its next major statement in December.

Rand believes offshore investors may be misreading the political situation. Currently nationalist New Zealand First leader Winston Peters, who holds the balance of power, is talking to the conservative National Party and centre-left Labour about forming a coalition government.

"Offshore, the politics isn't in people's face so they are not paying attention to it. The assumption offshore, which I think is erroneous, is that if there is a National-New Zealand First coalition government, which is what the market is betting on now, then nothing will change.
"That is obviously wrong because there is no way Peters will go into coalition without some major concessions," Rand said.

Gareth Morgan, economist with private forecaster Infometrics, said overseas investors are looking to make profits on a big rally in New Zealand short-term interest rates and equities when the Reserve Bank eases.
"They're anticipating the Reserve Bank to validate the rally in the bond market that we have already had. They are piling in at the short end in anticipation of a rally there," he said.
The election was the catalyst for people to act.

"The only thing that was holding people back prior to the election was the scare that there would be some sort of wacko lefty group holding the balance of power which could send New Zealand's policies back to the dinosaur age. That was the fear.
"If you take away that fear, then all you have is this huge interest difference between us and the rest of the world staring you in the face. It's too much to resist," Morgan said.
But Morgan also believes the rise in the currency will cause intolerable pain in the tradeable sector.
"We are achieving our low inflation by screwing to death our export sector. At the end of the day the jobs are in the export sector," he said.
But as long as the Reserve Bank is mandated to keep inflation lower that everyone else in the world, New Zealand's real interest rates will be an irresistible attraction to foreign investors.
However, New Zealand First leader Peters is determined to see the kiwi lower and he has some sympathy from markets as well as exporters.
Even technically, the Kiwi is seen as overbought.

"We will see a multi-year top shortly. I can't tell what the zenith will be but it is very close," said ANZ technical analyst Mark Elliott, who drew parallels with the June 1988 peak that was followed by a sharp fall.

"When we do see an aggressive price rejection from these new highs, it will be a top that won't be seen for many years. All the warning signs are there, especially the blow-off type price action we are seeing at the moment. It's just bursting higher in a vacuum of supply." -- Wellington newsroom 64 4 4734 746
